lessons.title: F and J, the index fingers
lessons.tip: Welcome! Rest your index fingers on F (left hand) and J (right hand). These are your anchor keys: you can feel a small bump on each. Don't look at the keyboard. Trust your muscle memory.

tuto.intro: Welcome to your very first lesson! Spend 30 seconds on the basics of touch typing. It will make everything that follows much easier.

rules.d: Rest all eight fingers on the middle row. Your index fingers sit on F and J, where you can feel the small bumps. They tell you where you are without looking.

rules.t: Keep your eyes on the screen
rules.d: Don't look at your fingers. Once you stop checking the keyboard, you start building the muscle memory that makes you properly fast.
Type F with your left index finger and J with your right. After every keystroke, your finger returns to its home key.
Type slowly and accurately. Every mistake builds a bad habit. Speed will follow once the movement is memorised.

tuto.tip: Goal: lock in the position of your two index fingers by typing only F and J. Don't force it. Aim for a steady rhythm rather than speed.

lessons.title: D and K, the middle fingers
lessons.tip: Your middle fingers rest naturally on D and K, right next to your index fingers. Keep your index fingers on F and J as anchors. Every finger returns to its home key after each keystroke.

tuto.intro: Now you add your middle fingers. D and K sit right beside your index fingers, on the same home row.

rules.d: Your left middle finger covers D and your right covers K. They sit naturally on these keys, right next to F and J.
Don't move your index fingers. They stay on F and J while your middle fingers type. That is how you find your way back without looking.
A small press is enough. Don't lift your whole hand. Let the finger go down and come back up to its place.

tuto.tip: Goal: play F D K J from memory, keeping all four fingers close to their home keys.

lessons.title: S and L, the ring fingers
lessons.tip: Your ring fingers cover S and L. That makes six fingers in place. Keep your fingers gently curved, ready to strike without lifting your wrist.

tuto.intro: Place your ring fingers on S (left) and L (right). You now have six fingers resting on the home row.

rules.d: Your ring fingers are less nimble than your index and middle fingers. That's normal. Go slowly: accuracy comes before speed.
Keep your fingers gently curved, as if resting on a small ball. Your wrist stays relaxed and doesn't sink onto the desk.
After every S or L, the ring finger goes back to its place. Your index fingers on F and J stay your guide.

tuto.tip: Goal: type S and L without twisting your hand, returning to the home row each time.

lessons.title: Q and M, the little fingers
lessons.tip: Your little fingers are the weakest, and that's normal. Q is on the left, M on the right. Don't turn your whole wrist: just let the little finger stretch a little.

tuto.intro: Now for your little fingers: Q on the left, M on the right. They are the hardest to tame.

rules.d: At first your little fingers lack strength and accuracy. Everyone starts this way, even the professionals. Be patient.
Stretch only the little finger towards Q or M. If you pivot your wrist, your other fingers lose their place.
Your little finger tends to hover in the air. Return it to its home key as soon as it has typed.

tuto.tip: Goal: wake up your little fingers without breaking your home position. Go slowly and steadily.

lessons.title: G and H, the inner index fingers
lessons.tip: Your index fingers reach in towards the middle to type G and H. Keep the movement small: the finger slides, it doesn't jump. Return to F or J after each keystroke.

tuto.intro: G and H sit in the middle of the keyboard. Your index fingers stretch a little to reach them.

rules.d: Your left index finger slides right to G, and your right index finger slides left to H. It's a small sideways movement, not a leap.
Straight after G or H, bring your index finger back to its home key. These are the keys furthest from your starting position.
G is always typed with the left index finger, H always with the right. Keep this rule firmly in mind.

tuto.tip: Goal: cover the whole middle of the home row without moving your other fingers.

lessons.title: Review: the whole home row
lessons.keys: q s d f g h j k l m
lessons.tip: A full review of the home row. It is the most important row: the base of every movement, the place your fingers keep coming back to. Take your time. Steadiness matters more than speed.

tuto.intro: You now know the whole home row, the most important row on the keyboard.

rules.d: Your fingers set off from here and come back after every keystroke. Mastering it is the basis for typing any word without looking.
This exercise mixes all ten keys. If you hesitate, slow down. The aim is to find each key from memory, not to type fast.
Between keystrokes, feel that all eight fingers have returned to the home row.

tuto.tip: Goal: pass the whole home row with your fingers anchored and your eyes on the screen.

lessons.text: sdf jkl qsd mlk fgh jhg dsq klm gfd hjk sqm fdg lkj qsdf hjkl ghfd mlqs

lessons.title: R and U, your first real words
lessons.tip: R is typed by your left index finger, stretching upwards, and U by your right. Well done: with these two keys you can already make real words! Keep your eyes on the screen.

tuto.intro: You move up to the top row. With R and U, you will type your very first real English words.

rules.d: Your left index finger stretches up for R, and your right for U. The finger rises one row, then drops straight back to F or J.
Only the index finger moves. The other seven fingers stay on the home row. It's your safety net so you don't need to look.
rug, fur, mum, full... You can already write whole words. Read the whole word before typing it, rather than letter by letter.

tuto.tip: Goal: reach up to R and U without taking your eyes off the screen or lifting your other fingers from the home row.

lessons.text: full mum us rug fur rush drum surf rugs furs mug jug hug gum sum dull rug fur rush drum surf

lessons.title: E and I, more and more words
lessons.tip: E is the most common letter in English, so your left middle finger will be busy. I is typed by the right middle finger. From this lesson you can write dozens of real words, so use them to smooth out your movement.

tuto.intro: E and I join in. E is the most common letter in English, so it will be your most used key.

rules.d: Your left middle finger rises to E, and your right to I. As with R and U, it's a quick trip up to the top row and back.
E turns up constantly in English words. Take extra care with this movement: mastering it will transform your speed.
he, is, here, girl, fish, field... Dozens of words are now possible. Aim for smooth typing rather than a performance.

tuto.tip: Goal: make E and I automatic, with a smooth movement and a return to the home row every time.

lessons.text: he is here if she is here girl did file red desk fire fish milk seed field ruler

lessons.title: Z and O, new words
lessons.tip: Z is typed by the left ring finger (top row) and O by the right ring finger. Try reading the next word while you type the current one. This is called reading ahead.

tuto.intro: Z and O complete the ring-finger keys on the top row. Your vocabulary grows again.

rules.d: Your left ring finger rises to Z, and your right to O. These fingers are weaker, so a small, precise movement is enough.
Read the next word while typing the current one. Reading ahead is what makes typing smooth and continuous.
zero, zoo, size, horse, good... Keep a steady rhythm from word to word and don't forget the spaces.

tuto.tip: Goal: type Z and O cleanly and start reading ahead to the next word.

lessons.text: zero zoo size fizz freeze seize zoo size zero fizz horse should do good

lessons.title: A and P, much richer words
lessons.tip: A is typed by the left little finger (top row) and P by the right. Little fingers on the top row need a slight stretch. Keep your wrist steady and let the finger do the work.

tuto.intro: A and P are the little-finger keys on the top row. With them, almost the whole alphabet is yours.

rules.d: Your left little finger reaches A, and your right reaches P. This is one of the most demanding movements, so go slowly.
Don't lift your whole hand to help your little finger. Your wrist stays steady and only the little finger stretches.
apple, paper, please, salad... Your vocabulary is now properly varied. Try longer words without looking.

tuto.tip: Goal: master A and P without losing your position, even if your little fingers still lack strength.

lessons.text: apple paper pear page pupil push pull please plum poem soup keep sleep speak help jump ship shop salad glad dad

lessons.title: T and Y, words and short sentences
lessons.tip: T and Y are both typed by the index fingers: the left one stretches to T and the right one to Y. It's a mirror-image movement. At this stage, aim for a steady rhythm rather than rushing.

tuto.intro: T and Y finish the top row. Your index fingers are working again, towards the top centre of the keyboard.

rules.d: Your left index finger stretches to T and your right to Y. Both hands make the same movement in mirror image.
At this stage, aim for an even pace rather than bursts of speed. A steady rhythm means fewer mistakes.
After T or Y, your index finger returns to F or J. This habit of returning is the key to never losing your place.

tuto.tip: Goal: build T and Y into a smooth, even movement of both index fingers.

lessons.text: yes they type story tall lady happy sky grey story too hot the

lessons.title: Review: the whole top row
lessons.keys: a z e r t y u i o p
lessons.tip: You now master two full rows. In this review, concentrate on moving smoothly between rows. Going from the home row to the top row should happen without lifting your wrists from the desk.

tuto.intro: You now know two whole rows. This review mixes all the letters of the top row.

rules.t: Home row and top row, no jerks
rules.d: The challenge is no longer each key but the move between rows. Going from the home row up should feel smooth.
Don't lift your wrists to change row. Only your fingers go up and down.
Try reading two or three words ahead. Your brain prepares your fingers while you type.

tuto.tip: Goal: move between the home row and the top row without looking, with a smooth finger movement.

lessons.text: girl quiet pupil happy horse tired soup hot lady late story tall type they yes the

lessons.title: C and the comma
lessons.tip: You're starting on the bottom row. C is typed by the left middle finger (a little lower than D), and the comma by the right middle finger. For the bottom row, let your fingers curl down naturally. Your wrist may drop slightly.

tuto.intro: You're starting on the bottom row. C and the comma are your first keys below the home row.

rules.d: Your left middle finger drops to C, below D. The comma is on the right side. The movement goes down, not sideways.
For the bottom row, your wrist may drop very slightly, but always return to the home position afterwards.
A comma sticks to the word before it, then a space follows. Tidy punctuation makes your writing easy to read.

tuto.tip: Goal: reach down to C and the comma without losing the home row, with a relaxed wrist.

lessons.text: cake, cheese, rice, coffee, tea, milk, soup, salad, coat, cold, cool, duck, car, cat

lessons.title: V and N, everyday words
lessons.tip: V is typed by the left index finger (bottom row) and N by the right. Your index fingers handle a lot of keys, so practise switching quickly between rows without losing the F and J reference.

tuto.intro: V and N drop below your index fingers. With them, almost all everyday vocabulary is within reach.

rules.d: Your left index finger drops to V, and your right to N. Your index fingers now cover three rows: top, home and bottom.
Your index fingers work hard. Practise moving from one row to another without losing F and J as your reference.
seven, river, village, never, heavy... You are now writing very common words. Aim for a continuous movement.

tuto.tip: Goal: reach down to V and N and smooth out the switch between rows.

lessons.text: five, seven, nine, ten, even, never, over, river, village, valley, visit, heavy, glove, evening, give

lessons.title: X and the semicolon
lessons.tip: X is typed by the left ring finger on the bottom row: it's a diagonal movement you won't use often. The semicolon is on the right side. Take time to locate each key before you speed up.

tuto.intro: X and the semicolon are rarer keys, but you need them for truly complete typing.

rules.d: Your left ring finger drops diagonally to X. It's an unusual movement, so do it slowly to memorise it.
You won't use these keys often. If you hesitate, feel for the key with your finger rather than looking.
It joins two closely related ideas in a sentence. Like the comma, it sticks to the word, then a space follows.

tuto.tip: Goal: memorise where X and the semicolon are, without looking at the keyboard.

lessons.text: six; fox; mix; next; text; exit; taxi; extra; relax; exam

lessons.title: W and the colon
lessons.tip: W is typed by the left little finger on the bottom row, and the colon by the right ring finger, on the right of the home row: a key of its own, no Shift needed, right next to the semicolon.

tuto.intro: W arrives at the bottom left, and the colon adds another punctuation key on the right, with no Shift.

rules.d: Your left little finger drops to W, at the bottom left. Keep your wrist steady: only the little finger stretches.
The colon is typed directly, without Shift. It's a key of its own, right next to the semicolon.
As always, each key has its own finger. Don't move your whole hand for a single keystroke.

tuto.tip: Goal: place W and the colon, each with the right finger, without tensing your hand.

lessons.text: drinks: tea, water, milk; food: rice, soup, cheese; colours: red, white, grey; weather: wet, warm, wind; animals: owl, hen, fox; fruit: apple, plum, pear; time: day, week

lessons.title: B and the exclamation mark
lessons.tip: B is typed by the left index finger on the bottom row, towards the centre. The exclamation mark can sit in different places depending on your keyboard, so look at the keyboard shown on screen. You now cover all 26 letters of the alphabet. That's a big milestone! Any real text is now within reach.

tuto.intro: B completes the alphabet and the exclamation mark adds some feeling. A real milestone: you will have all 26 letters.

rules.d: Your left index finger stretches towards the centre, then drops to B. It's a fairly wide movement, so get back to F quickly.
Its position (and whether you need Shift) depends on your AZERTY layout. Follow the keyboard shown on screen rather than a fixed rule.
With B, you know the whole alphabet. From here on, any English word is within your reach.

tuto.tip: Goal: place B and the exclamation mark, and enjoy having completed the full alphabet.

lessons.text: big boat! blue bike! bad bear! brown bird! black book! baby boy! bus! bag!

lessons.title: Review: all 26 letters together
lessons.tip: All the letters are here. The aim of this review is not to look at the keyboard at all. If you hesitate over a key, pause, picture where it is, then strike. Don't look: feel for it with your finger.

tuto.intro: You now have every letter of the alphabet at your fingertips. This review mixes them all.

rules.d: The only goal here is never to look at the keyboard. This is the moment to check that your muscle memory holds.

rules.t: Feel for it with your finger
rules.d: If you hesitate over a key, don't look down. Picture it from F and J, then strike.
It's better to type slowly without looking than quickly while cheating. Speed will come, and the good habit stays.

tuto.tip: Goal: write with all 26 letters without a single glance at the keyboard.

lessons.text: the quick brown fox can jump over the big dog; one boy can watch from the bus, but we wait: next stop, the zoo!

lessons.title: Rhythm and short words
lessons.tip: Type these short words as if you were counting: one movement, one beat. Keep the same tempo from start to finish, without speeding up or slowing down.

tuto.intro: You now have every letter in hand. Next comes rhythm: chaining short, even words to smooth out your typing.

rules.d: Type words at a constant pace, like a metronome. Being regular is better than quick jerks.
Your brain doesn't type letter by letter but in small groups. "in and out" feels like one single movement.
Keep your shoulders and wrists loose. Tension breaks your rhythm and tires your hands.

tuto.tip: Goal: find a steady, smooth rhythm on short English words.

lessons.text: up and down, in and out, on and off, here and there, now and then, one two three, six seven eight

lessons.title: Essential little words
lessons.tip: Little everyday words turn up in every sentence. Aim for a single burst per word, without thinking letter by letter.

tuto.intro: Little everyday words (the, and, of, to, in...) turn up in every English sentence. Make them automatic and you gain speed everywhere.

rules.d: These words make up a huge share of any English text. The more automatic they are, the faster you type overall.
Try to type each little word in a single burst, without thinking letter by letter.
Read the next word while your fingers finish the last one.

tuto.tip: Goal: type the little everyday words without hesitation, as reflexes.

lessons.text: the, and, of, to, in, is, it, you, that, he, was, for, on, are, with, his, at, be, this, have, from, but, not

lessons.title: Common everyday words
lessons.tip: Everyday words (meals and drinks). Don't suddenly slow down on a longer word: keep an even pace across the whole line.

tuto.intro: Now we widen to common everyday words. The more words you have on autopilot, the smoother your typing becomes.

rules.d: A word repeated often enough ends up typing itself. That is the aim: it frees your head to think about the meaning.
Don't suddenly slow down on a longer word. Keep an even pace across the whole line.
If a word often trips you up, slow down on it for a few repetitions, then pick the tempo back up.

tuto.tip: Goal: chain common words together with ease and a steady rhythm.

lessons.text: bread, butter, cheese, rice, soup, salad, milk, coffee, tea, sugar, honey, apple, orange, cake, water

lessons.title: Everyday vocabulary
lessons.tip: Longer, more concrete words. Break them into small movements (kit-chen, gar-den) and keep an even rhythm from start to finish.

tuto.intro: Longer, more concrete words. A chance to hold your rhythm on words with several syllables.

rules.d: A long word is typed as a string of small movements. gar-den, kit-chen, com-pu-ter: think in chunks.
The longer the word, the more a mistake costs. Keep your typing clean rather than rushed.

rules.t: Look ahead to the end of the word
rules.d: While you type the start, your eyes have already caught the end. Let your fingers follow.

tuto.tip: Goal: type longer words without breaking your rhythm or your accuracy.

lessons.text: kitchen, garden, window, teacher, computer, mountain, airport, holiday, evening, morning, village, children, neighbour

lessons.title: First natural sentences
lessons.tip: You're typing real sentences. Read in small groups of words and keep a continuous movement, commas and semicolons included.

tuto.intro: You move on to real sentences. The challenge is no longer the key but the flow from one end of the sentence to the other.

rules.d: Read and type in small groups (the cat / is / on the mat) rather than one isolated word at a time.
The space bar is hit with your thumb, without breaking the rhythm. It's the most used key on the keyboard.
The comma, semicolon and exclamation mark stick to the last word, then a space follows.

tuto.tip: Goal: type whole sentences in one continuous, smooth movement.

lessons.text: it is cold today, so we stay at home; my sister makes tea, and we eat bread and cheese; the cat is on the mat!

lessons.title: Capitals: left hand (right Shift)
lessons.tip: For a letter typed by your left hand, hold the right Shift key with your right little finger, strike the letter, then let go.

tuto.intro: A capital letter means holding Shift while you strike the letter. For left-hand letters, you use the right Shift key.

rules.d: For a letter typed by your left hand (A Z E R T Q S D F G W C V B), hold the RIGHT Shift with your right little finger. Your two hands share the work.
Press Shift, keep it down, strike the letter, then release. There's no need to do it all in one sharp move.

rules.t: Avoid the Shift on the same side
rules.d: Using the Shift on the same side as the letter twists your hand. The habit to build: always use the opposite hand.

tuto.tip: Goal: type left-hand capitals with the right Shift, without twisting your hand.

lessons.text: Bread, Cake, Dad, Eat, Fish, Garden, Queen, Read, Sit, Table, Water, Zoo, Visit, Apple, Bag

lessons.title: Capitals: right hand (left Shift)
lessons.tip: For a letter typed by your right hand, hold the left Shift key with your left little finger. It's the mirror image of the last lesson.

tuto.intro: This time, the right-hand letters. You hold the LEFT Shift with your left little finger.

rules.t: Left Shift for the right hand
rules.d: For a letter typed by your right hand (Y U I O P H J K L M N), your left little finger holds the left Shift. It's the mirror image of the last lesson.
One hand holds Shift, the other strikes. This split keeps both hands in place without any contortions.
A capital shouldn't break your pace. With practice, Shift becomes a natural, smooth movement.

tuto.tip: Goal: type right-hand capitals with the left Shift, keeping your hands settled.

lessons.text: Hat, Ice, Jump, Keep, Lamp, Moon, Night, Open, Pear, Under, Yes, Orange, Hello, King, Nose

lessons.title: Names and towns
lessons.tip: In English, first names, towns and countries always start with a capital letter. Just one, at the start of the word.

tuto.intro: Now apply capitals to real names: towns and first names. Only one capital, at the start of the word.

rules.d: Only the first letter takes Shift. Release Shift straight away to type the rest of the word in lower case.
Towns and first names start with a capital letter: London, Anna, Oxford. It's a rule, not an option.
Prepare your little finger on Shift just before the letter. The movement is cleaner when you see it coming.

tuto.tip: Goal: capitalise first names and towns, with Shift on the first letter only.

lessons.text: Bath, Leeds, Bristol, Oxford, York, Wales, Anna, Emma, Paul, Tom, Kate, Lucy, Harry, Sam, Ben

lessons.title: Sentences with capitals
lessons.tip: A sentence starts with a capital letter, and the pronoun "I" always takes one, wherever it appears in the sentence.

tuto.intro: The final step: capitals in context, at the start of every sentence. You haven't learned the full stop yet, so here exclamation marks and commas separate the sentences.

rules.d: Every sentence starts with a capital letter. Think about it as you type, not afterwards.
In English, "I" is always a capital, even in the middle of a sentence: "I am Anna", "and I live here".
Glance over your work to check that your sentence starts and proper names have their capitals. It shows you take care.

tuto.tip: Goal: use a capital at the start of sentences and on proper names without breaking your rhythm.

lessons.text: I am Anna; I live in Leeds, and Paul is here; Tom is late, but Kate can swim, and Harry can run!

lessons.title: The full stop and the comma
lessons.tip: The full stop and the comma stick to the word before them, with no space first, then a space follows.

tuto.intro: The full stop and the comma are the two most used marks. Placing them well makes any text easy to read.

rules.d: The full stop and the comma stick to the word before them (no space before), then a space follows.

rules.t: The full stop ends the sentence
rules.d: After a full stop, the next sentence starts with a capital letter. The comma marks a short pause.
Punctuation is part of typing. Don't stop dead: type the mark, then the space, in one flow.

tuto.tip: Goal: place the full stop and comma with no space before and one space after.

lessons.text: Dad is here. Mum is here. Anna is glad. The cat is on the mat. Tom has a red bag. We eat bread, cheese and honey.

lessons.title: Question and exclamation marks
lessons.tip: In English, ? and ! stick to the word before them: no space before, then one space after.

tuto.intro: The question mark and the exclamation mark set the tone: a question, or some feeling.

rules.d: On this keyboard, the ? is typed with Shift. Hold Shift with the opposite hand, then strike the mark.
In English, ? and ! stick to the last word: "Where is Tom?". Only one space, after the mark.
Use ? to ask and ! to exclaim. One is enough: avoid piling up exclamation marks.

tuto.tip: Goal: type ? and ! stuck to the word, with a space only after.

lessons.text: Where is Tom? Who is that? What is this? Is Dad here? Can we go? Why not? Yes, we can! Hello!

lessons.title: Colon and semicolon
lessons.tip: In English, the colon and the semicolon stick to the word before them, with a space only after.

tuto.intro: The colon introduces, the semicolon links. Two tools for building richer sentences.

rules.d: It brings in a list or an explanation: "Here is the list:". No space before, one space after.
It separates two closely related ideas, or two groups in a list, without ending the sentence. Same spacing as the colon.
On this keyboard, ; and : sit side by side on the right. Learn where they are so you don't mix them up.

tuto.tip: Goal: use the colon and semicolon stuck to the word, with a space after.

lessons.text: Here is the list: bread, milk, eggs; tea, sugar, honey; apples, plums, pears. Three rules: be kind, be quiet, be early.

lessons.title: The apostrophe and the hyphen
lessons.tip: The apostrophe and the hyphen stick to the words, with no space around them: don't, one-way.

tuto.intro: In English, the apostrophe is mostly used in contractions (it's, don't, I'm) and the hyphen in compound words (one-way, mother-in-law).

rules.d: It stands in for missing letters in a contraction: it's (it is), don't (do not), I'm (I am). No spaces around it.
It links the parts of a compound word: one-way, check-in, mother-in-law. No spaces around it.
Small but very common. Learn where they are so you can type them without slowing down.

tuto.tip: Goal: place the apostrophe and hyphen stuck to the words, with no space around them.

lessons.text: one-way, check-in, part-time, mother-in-law, so-so, well-known; it's, don't, can't, isn't, we're, that's

lessons.title: Brackets
lessons.tip: Every bracket you open must be closed, and there's no space just inside it: (like this).

tuto.intro: Brackets add a detail in the middle of a sentence. You learn to open them and close them.

rules.d: Every bracket you open must be closed. No space just inside: (like this).
Depending on your keyboard, ( and ) sometimes need Shift, so hold Shift with the opposite hand. The movement for your keyboard is shown above.

rules.t: A space before, a space after
rules.d: Put a space before the opening bracket and one after the closing bracket, except before a comma or full stop.

tuto.tip: Goal: open and close brackets in pairs, without forgetting any.

lessons.text: Dad (tired) and Mum (happy) are here (at last). We have a cat (grey), a dog (brown) and a hen (white).

lessons.title: Punctuation in real text
lessons.tip: In real text, every mark has its rule: stick each mark to the word before it, then put a space after.

tuto.intro: Now we bring all the punctuation together in real text. It's the test closest to real writing.

rules.d: Commas, full stops, colons, brackets... It all arrives together. Stay calm and follow the spacing rules.
Reminder: never a space before , . ; : ? ! but always one after. Apostrophes and hyphens stay stuck to the words.
Spot the punctuation coming by reading the text ahead: you prepare the right finger and the right Shift.

tuto.tip: Goal: punctuate a real text cleanly, following the English spacing rules.

lessons.text: Hello, Tom! Where are you? We're at the station (platform two); it's cold, so don't wait. It's a well-known stop: come in!

lessons.title: 4 5 6 7: close to the index fingers
lessons.tip: Digits are typed with Shift held down. 4 and 5: left index finger, with the right Shift. 6 and 7: right index finger, with the left Shift.

tuto.intro: You move up to the number row, starting in the centre with 4 5 6 7, the closest to your index fingers. On this keyboard, digits are typed with Shift held down: without Shift, the key gives a different symbol, which is no use here.

rules.d: Hold Shift with the hand opposite to the typing finger: right Shift for 4 and 5 (left index finger), left Shift for 6 and 7 (right index finger).
Type 4 and 5 with your left index finger and 6 and 7 with your right. Your index fingers stretch up to the digits, then drop back.
After every digit, bring your index finger back to F or J. It's the landmark that stops you getting lost up there.

tuto.tip: Goal: reach 4 5 6 7 with your index fingers, using Shift, without looking down.

lessons.text: Bus 45 leaves at 6.57; bus 67 leaves at 7.46. Room 54, room 65, room 74, room 46, seat 47, seat 56, seat 57.

lessons.title: 3 and 8: one step further
lessons.tip: Type 3 with your left middle finger and 8 with your right, always with Shift held by the opposite hand.

tuto.intro: Now we widen to the middle fingers: 3 on the left, 8 on the right, right beside the digits you know.

rules.d: Type 3 with your left middle finger (right Shift) and 8 with your right middle finger (left Shift). They carry on outwards from your index fingers' work.
Find your way from the centre: 4-5-6-7 in the middle, then 3 and 8 right beside them. The row builds up step by step.
The further up you go, the more the return to the home row matters. Come back to the middle row after every digit.

tuto.tip: Goal: add 3 and 8 with your middle fingers, without losing the centre.

lessons.text: Flat 38 is on floor 3; flat 83 is on floor 8. The bus leaves at 8.38 and 3.38, from stop 3 or stop 8.

lessons.title: 2 and 9: the ring fingers
lessons.tip: Type 2 with your left ring finger and 9 with your right: stretch the finger gently, then return to rest.

tuto.intro: Now the ring fingers: 2 on the left, 9 on the right. You're getting close to the edges of the row.

rules.d: 2 (left ring finger, right Shift) and 9 (right ring finger, left Shift) need a longer stretch. These fingers are weaker, so go slowly.
Keep the same rule: the hand that isn't typing holds Shift. It soon becomes automatic.
The further from the centre, the more mistakes creep in. Slow and right beats fast and wrong.

tuto.tip: Goal: reach 2 and 9 with your ring fingers, without looking.

lessons.text: There are 29 pupils in class 2. Read page 92, page 29 and page 9. Bus 22 leaves at 9.29, bus 99 at 2.29.

lessons.title: 1 and 0: the little fingers
lessons.tip: Type 1 with your left little finger and 0 with your right: let the finger stretch out without moving your whole hand.

tuto.intro: The ends of the row: 1 at the far left, 0 at the far right, for your little fingers.

rules.d: 1 (left little finger) and 0 (right little finger) are the furthest digits. Your little fingers stretch a long way.
To reach the edges, don't move your whole hand. Let the little finger stretch out and keep the rest anchored.
With 1 and 0, you cover the whole number row. All that's left is to chain them together.

tuto.tip: Goal: reach 1 and 0 with your little fingers, keeping your hand steady.

lessons.text: I have 10 pencils, 100 pens and 1 ruler. The date is 10 March. Room 101 is open until 10.10; flat 1 is free.

lessons.title: All the digits together
lessons.tip: Each digit has its finger, and the other hand keeps Shift held: 1 2 3 then 4 5 with the left hand, 6 7 then 8 9 0 with the right.

tuto.intro: Now we chain all ten digits. Each has its finger: time to link everything up.

rules.d: 1-2-3: left little, ring and middle fingers. 4-5: left index finger. 6-7: right index finger. 8-9-0: right middle, ring and little fingers.
The number row is the highest, so the trip there and back is long. Keep a clean movement, without looking.
Digits are often a weak point. Practise them calmly: very useful for codes, dates and amounts.

tuto.tip: Goal: chain 0 to 9 from memory, each digit with the right finger.

lessons.title: Digits in real text
lessons.tip: In British English, a date is written "12 March 2026" and a time "8:30": the day first, then the month.

tuto.intro: We mix digits and letters in real text: numbers, times, dates. This is everyday use.

rules.d: The challenge: going from the letter rows to the number row without losing your bearings. Always come back to F and J.
Times, dates, headcounts, room numbers... Digits in context are everywhere in real life.
One mistake in a number changes everything. With digits, accuracy matters even more than speed.

tuto.tip: Goal: type digits and letters mixed together without hesitating or looking.

lessons.text: There are 42 pupils in 3 classes of 14. Bus 12 leaves at 8.30. Room 105. The date is 12 March 2026.

lessons.title: @ and #: email and hashtag
lessons.tip: How you type @ and # depends on your keyboard: the movement is shown just below. Keep your fingers on the home row between symbols.

tuto.intro: Symbols like @ and # need a key combination that changes between keyboards. The one for yours is shown just below.

rules.d: Depending on your keyboard, a symbol is typed directly, with Shift, or with AltGr (the key to the right of the space bar, held with your right thumb).
The @ sign links the name and the domain of an address: anna@school.example. You need it every day.
The hash sign is used for keywords on social media and in code.

tuto.tip: Goal: produce @ and # with the right movement, without breaking your home position.

lessons.text: anna@school.example #bath @tom #team info@bank.example #rain @kate #happy hello@club.example @sam #sunny #cake

lessons.title: Brackets () and square brackets []
lessons.tip: Brackets and square brackets come in pairs: type the pair, then go back and write in the middle.

tuto.intro: Brackets and square brackets come in pairs: you learn to always open AND close.

rules.d: A bracket or square bracket you open must always be closed. Type the pair, then go back and write in the middle.
You already know ( and ) from the lesson on brackets. Here we mix them with square brackets.
Square brackets [ ] need a key combination (the movement for your keyboard is shown above). Useful for code and lists.

tuto.tip: Goal: open and close brackets and square brackets, without forgetting any.

lessons.text: list[0] list[1] total(2) score[3] items[4] (ok) [end] count(5) index[i] page[6] (yes) [no]

lessons.title: / and |: paths and pipes
lessons.tip: The slash / separates the parts of an address or a path. The vertical bar | links two commands.

tuto.intro: The slash / and the vertical bar | are used in web addresses, file paths and commands.

rules.d: The slash separates the parts of a web address or a path: www.school.example/news, home/anna.
The vertical bar needs a key combination. In computing, it links two commands: ls | grep file.
These two signs are everywhere once you work with the web or a terminal. Learn their combinations.

tuto.tip: Goal: type / and | for paths and commands.

lessons.text: www.school.example/news ls | grep file | sort | head | more yes/no and/or home/anna a/b | c/d left | right

lessons.title: * = +: sums and code
lessons.tip: In a simple formula, operators are often stuck together: x*y+z. Feel the rhythm key by key.

tuto.intro: The operators * = + are used in sums and code. You chain them together in expressions.

rules.d: * to multiply, + to add, = for the result or an assignment: 2*3=6, a+b=c.
Their position changes between keyboards: look at the movement for your keyboard, shown above.
In a simple expression, operators are often stuck together: x*y+z. Feel the rhythm key by key.

tuto.tip: Goal: chain * = + in expressions, without hesitating over the right movement.

lessons.text: 2*3=6 a+b=c x*y+z=0 total=price*8 score=time*9+1 count=a+b+c speed=5*2 4+5=9 area=4*7=28

lessons.title: % and _: rates and variables
lessons.tip: The % sticks to the number (50%). The underscore _ joins words without a space in technical names.

tuto.intro: The percent sign % and the underscore _ often turn up in figures and technical names.

rules.d: It sticks to the number: 50%, 100%.
The underscore joins words without a space in technical names: my_name, file_name.
% and _ are mostly useful in computing and data. Learn where they are so you don't slow down.

tuto.tip: Goal: place % and _ without looking.

lessons.text: 50% 75% my_name file_name 100% top_speed 20% word_count 5% pass_mark 90% tea_time

lessons.title: {} and <>: code and HTML
lessons.tip: Curly brackets and angle brackets come in pairs: open, write, then close.

tuto.intro: Curly brackets {} and angle brackets <> are the symbols of code and HTML. They also come in pairs.

rules.d: Curly brackets { } wrap blocks of code: {code}. How you type them depends on your keyboard (shown above).
Angle brackets < > open and close HTML tags. Depending on your keyboard, > is typed with Shift: the movement is shown above.
Like brackets, curly brackets and tags are opened AND closed: <p>text</p>, {return x}.

tuto.tip: Goal: open and close curly brackets and angle brackets.

lessons.text:
hello

go {code} {start} {a} {b} {c} {end}

lessons.title: "" and ~: strings and paths
lessons.tip: The straight quotation mark wraps text in code. The tilde ~ stands for the home folder: ~/work.

tuto.intro: Straight quotation marks and the tilde ~ are used for strings of text and system paths.

rules.d: The straight quotation mark (") wraps strings in code. How you type it depends on your keyboard (shown above).
The tilde stands for the home folder on Linux and Mac: ~/music.
You rarely need these two signs in everyday writing, but they are essential in programming and at the terminal.

tuto.tip: Goal: type the straight quotation mark and ~ without hesitating.

lessons.text: "hello" "world" ~/music ~/school "name": "Anna" ~tom ~/book "city": "York" ~/work ~/home

lessons.title: \ and `: code and terminal
lessons.tip: The backslash and the backtick are purely technical: you find them in code, Windows paths and the terminal.

tuto.intro: The backslash and the backtick are purely technical symbols, common in code.

rules.d: It separates folders on Windows and marks special characters in code.
The backtick wraps inline code and variables in programming. On some keyboards, you have to press the key then the space bar.
You will only use them in code or at the terminal. Learn them if you program, otherwise just remember that they exist.

tuto.tip: Goal: find the backslash and the backtick and type them without looking.

lessons.text: C:\Work\Anna `copy` \n \t `name` C:\School\Tom `open file` \r\n `ls -a`

lessons.title: Review: all the symbols in text
lessons.tip: Before each symbol, ask yourself: direct, Shift or AltGr? This habit saves you time.

tuto.intro: We bring all the symbols together in one text mixing email, web, code and percentages. The big mix!

rules.d: Shift, AltGr, special keys... Every symbol has its movement. Use everything you've learned in the last two modules.
Before each symbol, work out: direct, Shift or AltGr? This habit saves you time.
Mastering symbols means typing an address, a bit of code or a formula without ever getting stuck.

tuto.tip: Goal: chain all the symbols in a real text, each combination at the right moment.

lessons.text: anna@school.example (2026) www.bank.example/help #leeds {open: true} <html> 50% a+b=c [end] ~/home "name" my_file | ls

lessons.title: Chaining short sentences
lessons.tip: Chain the sentences without a pause: the full stop, the space and the next capital are all part of the same movement.

tuto.intro: Time for speed. We chain short sentences to work on fluency from one end to the other.

rules.d: Don't stop between sentences. The full stop, the space and the capital letter flow in one movement.
Keep your eyes a step ahead of your fingers. That's the secret of fast, smooth typing.
Speed comes from suppleness, not force. Loosen your shoulders and wrists.

tuto.tip: Goal: chain short sentences with no dead time between them.

lessons.text: The sun is up. The birds sing. The tea is hot. We leave at eight, so let's go. Have a lovely day!

lessons.title: Natural medium sentences
lessons.tip: Type in groups of words that go together: the sentence becomes a series of small bursts.

tuto.intro: Longer sentences, as in real life. The aim: hold your rhythm over time.

rules.d: On a long sentence, don't freeze if you make a mistake. Correct it and set off again. Keeping going comes first.
Type in groups of words that go together, not one word at a time. The sentence becomes a series of small bursts.
The longer the sentence, the more a mistake costs. Aim for a speed you can hold cleanly.

tuto.tip: Goal: type a medium sentence in one flow, without losing your rhythm.

lessons.text: Every morning, she opens the window and sits down with a cup of tea before she starts work.

lessons.title: A full narrative paragraph
lessons.tip: A paragraph takes stamina. Settle into a comfortable rhythm and keep it up to the end.

tuto.intro: A whole paragraph to type. It's about stamina: keeping your concentration and steadiness to the end.

rules.d: A paragraph takes stamina. Settle into a comfortable rhythm that you can keep up without getting tired.
The longer the text, the stronger the urge to look at the keyboard. Keep your eyes up.
Commas, full stops and apostrophes are part of the flow. Fit them in without breaking your pace.

tuto.tip: Goal: type a full paragraph at an even pace, from start to finish.

lessons.text: Typing without looking at your hands takes patience, but every day of practice makes your fingers faster. It is simply a matter of habit.

lessons.title: A professional text
lessons.tip: In a business letter, take care over capitals, punctuation and digits: aim for zero mistakes.

tuto.intro: A professional-style text: an email or a letter, with an address. The kind of text you will really write.

rules.d: Polite phrases, capitals, neat punctuation: a professional text has no room for sloppiness.
Numbers, emails, @: you mix everything you've learned. It's the summing up of your training.
In a professional setting, accuracy matters as much as speed. Proofread in your head as you type.

tuto.tip: Goal: type a clean professional text, with letters, digits and symbols mixed together.

lessons.text: Dear Ms Clark, please find our offer attached. Do not hesitate to contact us by email: info@school.example. Kind regards, Anna Brown

lessons.title: A technical text with symbols
lessons.tip: Here, slow and exact is better than fast and sloppy: in code, a single mistake breaks everything.

tuto.intro: The full challenge: code and settings, with curly brackets, quotation marks, paths and digits.

rules.d: Curly brackets, quotation marks, colons, digits... This text uses Shift and AltGr non-stop. It's the most symbol-heavy test.
Work out in advance whether the next sign is direct, with Shift or with AltGr. Preparation avoids getting stuck.
In code, one mistake breaks everything. Here, slow and exact beats fast and sloppy.

tuto.tip: Goal: type a technical text mixing code, symbols and digits, cleanly.

lessons.text: The file settings.json: {"debug": false, "port": 3000}. Type: `npm start` in ~/project.

lessons.title: Speed sprint: a long text
lessons.tip: This is the final test: a clean sprint beats a sprint full of mistakes.

tuto.intro: The final test: a long text to type as fast and as accurately as you can. Give it everything!

rules.d: This is the moment to test your limits. Find your top speed while staying readable.
A clean sprint beats a sprint full of mistakes. Find the point where you go fast without slipping.
If you type this text without looking at the keyboard, you have reached the goal of KeyPace. Congratulations!

tuto.tip: Goal: type a long text at your top speed, without looking at the keyboard.

lessons.text: Typing fast comes with regular practice: train every day, keep your eyes on the screen, and let your fingers find their own way across the keys. Good luck!
